_about: Built by files/pirate-ship/economy/build-economy-data.py from skill-tree.json and GOODS.md. Do not edit by hand. Marks: source = a period record (GOODS.md Part 4); proposed = this session's placement for Rex; unsourced = Rex's design addition with no period source; estimate = worked out from sourced inputs (GOODS.md 1j). basePrice is null everywhere: the balance lane sets it; the sourced price text is beside it. The five per-settlement numbers (stock, consumption per day, target reserve, production per day, base price) belong to a ports file that does not exist yet (ALIGNMENT §10).
reviewed: Reviewed by Rex 2026-10-29 ('looks good'): the 40 skills, the placements and the occupations stand as the working set. 2026-10-29: spices, drugs, island foods and drinks added from the research (Brewing apart from Distilling, Rex 2026-10-29; imported-only goods listed). Later moves go through this JSON; the record of each split is in GOODS.md 3c and 3d. 2026-10-29: the rest of the Atlantic world added (GOODS.md 1l); origins tagged.
rowsNote: rows = the 65 cargo rows of GOODS.md Part 1 with their sourced kind, route, package, spoilage, price and type; goods = the engine's goods, one per recipe output, each pointing at its row

rows.name: Muscovado (brown) sugar
rows.route: Barbados and the other plantations → London, Bristol; also → New England for provisions
rows.package: "Caskes and Chests" (Ligon, 1650s); hogsheads (Pynchon 1665; Teach's haul 1718). Hogshead weight for 1650–1730: open. Hints: Ligon's curing pots each held about 30–35 lb, and a customs note says two Barbados hogsheads held "nine hundred weight"
rows.spoils: Drains in the hold. A loss of about 5% is reported, but from 19th-century evidence (late)
rows.value: 3d/lb on Barbados and 12d/lb in London (1650s). 33–47s per cwt in London (1701–05). 13s 6d–14s per cwt on Barbados (1685). 25s per cwt as a legal rate for payments, Jamaica 1661
rows.sources: L, PY, J, ML, JEH, C85, LAW, C61

rows.name: Clayed (white) sugar
rows.route: Barbados → London

rows.name: Refined loaf sugar
rows.route: Muscovado refined in Bristol and London. Pirates also took "loaf sugar" from a New England ship (1722)

rows.name: Molasses
rows.route: Reboiled on the plantation into rum or low-grade sugar; → London (91½ cwt in one month, 1681); → New England to be distilled

rows.name: Rum ("kill-devil")
rows.route: Barbados, Jamaica → sold on the island, → New England, carried as ship's stores
rows.package: gallon (unit of sale). Rundlet of 12–18½ gal (Pynchon). Hogshead (Lowther took 14, 1722). Puncheon of about 130 gal (old Britannica). Rum hogshead size: open
rows.value: half a crown (2s 6d) a gallon on Barbados (1650s)

rows.name: Ginger
rows.route: Barbados → London (122½ cwt in one month, 1681)

rows.name: Pimento (allspice)
rows.route: Jamaica → Britain (7,357 lb in one month, 1681)
rows.spoils: Must be kept dry from the dew (1778 source, late)

rows.name: Cotton wool
rows.route: Barbados and the plantations → London, New England

rows.name: Indigo
rows.route: English West Indies → London (168,807 lb, 1687–88); Puerto Rico → Jamaica, smuggled
rows.value: 8–9s/lb (Boston 1720, unverified). 3 rials/lb bought in Puerto Rico, worth 3s 6d/lb in Jamaica (1680s)

rows.name: Annatto ("otta")
rows.route: Puerto Rico → Jamaica

rows.name: Cacao (cocoa)
rows.route: Caracas coast → Holland on Dutch ships; Jamaica (small, crops failed in the 1660s); Martinique → France; → Spain on the fleets
rows.package: bag (Teach's haul: 145 bags, 1718). L'Olonnais took "120,000 weight"
rows.value: 4d/lb as a legal rate for payments, Jamaica 1661
rows.sources: D, PT, J, E, EB15, WHF

rows.name: Logwood
rows.route: Cut at Campeche and in the Bay of Honduras by men from Jamaica → London, Amsterdam, and by the 1720s via New England. Spain expelled the cutters from Campeche in 1717
rows.package: cwt, ton (725 cwt in one month, 1681)
rows.value: £5/ton in trade goods at the cutters' camps (1670s); £14–15/ton market price (Dampier's time); £25–30/ton sold from Jamaica (1670); £15/ton (1704 estimate); £13–15/ton Charleston (1715)

rows.name: Other dyewoods and hardwoods: fustic, brazeletto, Nicaragua wood, lignum vitae
rows.route: Plantations → London (1681)

rows.name: Mahogany
rows.route: Jamaica → Britain. A small trade after 1700, which grew once the 1721 Act took off the duty
rows.package: logs or planks: open. Described as "bulky and relatively light"
rows.value: Imports were worth £695 (1723) and £4,060 (1729). These are totals, not unit prices

rows.name: Tortoise shell
rows.route: Plantations → London (632 lb, 1681)

rows.name: Hides: cow, buff, cat
rows.route: Plantations → London (1681); Spanish Hispaniola ("vast quantities"); Cuba → the homeward fleet; Brazil (Roberts' prize, "Skins")

rows.name: Tallow
rows.route: Spanish Hispaniola

rows.name: Lime juice, aqua vitae
rows.route: Plantations → London (1,512 gal of lime juice and 944 gal of aqua vitae, 1681). Salt Tortuga rakers were supplied with lime juice

rows.name: Tobacco
rows.route: Virginia and Maryland → London. Also Cuba → the fleet, Brazil → Portugal, and Caribbean-grown tobacco → New England
rows.package: hogshead, about 1,000 lb (950–1,200 lb packed). The 1730 Virginia Act set the cask at no more than 48 in long and 30 in at the head, at least 800 lb net, with 30 lb allowed for the cask
rows.spoils: Dirt and stalks were sometimes packed in to add weight (quality, not spoilage)
rows.value: Planters got 10–20s per cwt (Virginia 1696) and at most 1s/lb (Maryland 1678); 4d/lb (Jamaica legal rate, 1661); 2s 6d/lb Charleston (1715); 8d/lb Newfoundland (1725); 1s 3d–1s 3¾d/lb in London lists (1715–20)
rows.sources: NPS, BIAS, VA30, E2, J, HV, CSP, TR

rows.name: Flour
rows.route: Springfield, New York, Philadelphia → Barbados and the islands. From 1680 to 1694 New York had a legal monopoly on bolting and packing flour for export
rows.package: barrel. 196 lb a barrel under later Virginia rules (1779, late); 1650–1730 weight open
rows.spoils: Weevils. New York inspected flour to protect its name

rows.name: Ship's biscuit ("bread")
rows.route: Connecticut Valley, New York, Philadelphia → the islands, and carried as ship's stores
rows.package: priced by the cwt. Container: open
rows.spoils: Weevils and maggots, though well-baked biscuit could keep for years (1788 source, late)

rows.name: Salt beef
rows.route: New England, Ireland (Dutch sloop "laden with Irish beef"), Holland, England, Virginia → Barbados and Curaçao
rows.package: barrel. Weight in the period: open
rows.spoils: Spoils if badly packed; Ligon says the beef reached Barbados sweet

rows.name: Salt pork
rows.route: Springfield → Barbados, by way of Hartford, New London and Boston
rows.package: barrel. A barrel arriving short was recorded (1662/63)

rows.name: Salt fish (dried cod)
rows.route: New England and Newfoundland → the islands, the low grade shipped on purpose as food for enslaved people
rows.spoils: It arrived "salt burnt, spotted, rotten" (period complaint)

rows.name: Pease
rows.route: Springfield → Barbados (1658)

rows.name: Oatmeal
rows.route: Ship's stores (Roberts took "10 Casks", c. 1720)

rows.name: Horses
rows.route: New England → Barbados and Antigua (from 1650)

rows.name: Lumber and barrel staves
rows.route: Connecticut River → Barbados (1649). Timber was needed to rebuild after hurricanes
rows.package: staves loose, lumber by the piece

rows.name: Shingles, hoops, oak plank
rows.route: Connecticut → the West Indies. Evidence only from a 1795 manifest (late); before 1730: open

rows.name: Rice
rows.route: South Carolina → Britain and its colonies, mostly re-shipped to northern Europe. Exports were 394,000 lb in 1700 and 19,973,000 lb in 1730
rows.package: barrel. 19,973,000 lb in 44,385 barrels (1730) is about 450 lb a barrel (calc); another source gives about 500 lb (18th c.). Tierce before 1730: not found

rows.name: Tar, pitch, turpentine (naval stores)
rows.route: Carolinas → England. The South Carolina boom of 1700–21 passed 40,000 barrels a year by 1720

rows.name: Deerskins ("Skinns")
rows.route: Carolina → England ("Seventeen ships ... laden with Rice, Skinns, Pitch and Tar", 1707)

rows.name: Linen and woollen cloth (lockram, canvas, dowlas, Scotch cloth, kentings, "Stuffs")
rows.route: England, Holland → Barbados, Virginia; Holland → the Spanish Main ("especially linen")
rows.package: cases, chests, trunks; bales (Roberts took "twenty five Bales of Goods")
rows.value: In England: dowlas (coarse linen) 1s 5d–1s 8d per ell, holland 2s 4d–2s 8d per yard (1690s); broadcloth 10s (1687) to 23s 6d (1655) per yard. At Albany: duffels 7s 6d per yard, Stroudwater £12 10s per piece (1698)
rows.sources: L, BR, D, J, TR, CSP

rows.name: Silk, chintz, muslin (Asian textiles)
rows.route: Asia → Europe → the Atlantic. Pirates took silk and linen at Maracaibo, chintzes from a French sloop (1721) and muslins from the Quedagh Merchant (1698, unverified)

rows.name: Clothing: hats, hose, shoes, boots, gloves
rows.route: England → Barbados

rows.name: Iron, steel, lead, brass, pewter (raw metal)
rows.route: England → Barbados; voyage iron → West Africa (row 53)
rows.value: Bar iron £16 10s–£18 per ton in London (1690s); Bilbao £15 10s and Swedish £16 10s per ton (London, 1728). Colonial price: open

rows.name: Iron tools and hardware: nails, hoes, axes, knives
rows.route: England → Virginia, Barbados

rows.name: Edged weapons and firearms: swords, muskets, great guns
rows.route: Europe → the colonies, → West Africa

rows.name: Gunpowder and shot
rows.route: England → Virginia ("one barrel of powder, five barrels of shot")
rows.package: barrel; quarter-cask (Low took six, 1722). Keg size: open
rows.spoils: Spoils if it gets damp (no source opened)

rows.name: Wine (French, Spanish, Madeira)
rows.route: Europe and Madeira → the colonies
rows.spoils: Ligon: wine in hogsheads loses its spirit in the heat
rows.value: Fayal wine £8 per pipe at Jamestown (1676). On Barbados, taverns were capped at 12d a quart for Madeira, Spanish and Portuguese wine and 8d for French (1672). In London, Madeira 6s 8d and sherry 8s a gallon (1697–98); claret £16 a hogshead (1699)

rows.name: Brandy
rows.route: France → the colonies (Lowther took "thirty Casks of Brandy", 1721); England → Virginia (100 gal)

rows.name: Beer ("good English Beer")
rows.route: England → Barbados

rows.name: Cheese, butter
rows.route: England, Holland → Barbados, Virginia
rows.package: firkin (butter; weight open); cheese by the cwt ("a hundred-weight of Gloucester cheese")
rows.spoils: Ligon: butter and cheese often spoil

rows.name: Meal ("Barrels of meale close put up")
rows.route: England → Barbados

rows.name: Candles
rows.route: England → Barbados

rows.name: Cordage, sailcloth, cables
rows.route: Europe → the colonies: no source opened. Pirates took them often (Part 2)

rows.name: Small wares: combs, pins, needles
rows.route: England → the colonies (Bonnet took "a few Combs, Pins and Needles", 1718)

rows.name: Medicines, surgeon's chest
rows.route: Europe → the colonies (trade route: open). Blackbeard demanded a chest at Charleston (1718)
rows.value: Charleston chest valued at £300–400; a surgeon's chest at 200–250 pieces of eight (Exquemelin, as a fixed share)

rows.name: Silver (bars, plate, pieces of eight)
rows.route: Potosí → Panama → Portobelo by mule → Spain on the galleons. Plate valued "ten pieces of eight to a pound" (Exquemelin)
rows.value: about 9 million pesos a year passed this way around 1600 (early)

rows.name: Gold, gold dust, coin (moidores)
rows.route: Brazil → Portugal (Roberts took 40,000 moidores); gold dust from West Africa

rows.name: Cochineal
rows.route: Oaxaca → Veracruz → Havana → Spain on the flota, 250,000–300,000 lb a year by 1600 (early); bought by Dutch dyers; second only to silver in value
rows.value: 18s–45s/lb in London (1714–29); 9–18 guilders per Amsterdam lb (1650–1728). Colonial price: open

rows.name: Pearls
rows.route: Taken from a Dutch pearl vessel, worth "above 100,000 pieces of eight" (Exquemelin)

rows.name: Enslaved Africans (the Middle Passage)
rows.route: West Africa → Barbados, Jamaica; by Dutch Curaçao → Spanish Cartagena and Portobelo. The Royal African Company carried 186,748 people on 652 voyages (1672–1731), and 16,077 died. Across the whole trade, 12.5 million were embarked and more than 1 million died crossing
rows.package: Men usually shackled in pairs below deck. The crossing took 6–8 weeks, or 13 or more in bad weather
rows.spoils: Deaths averaged 10–20%. The Hannibal (1693–95) lost 328 people, 47%
rows.value: Barbados average price £13.89 (1663) and £14.58 (1664); the RAC's 1663–64 sales averaged "a little over 16 pounds"
rows.sources: RAC, CW, DB2, HN, EL, D

rows.name: Voyage iron (bar iron)
rows.route: England (Bristol) → West Africa, used as currency and as raw metal. The RAC aimed to keep at least 1,000 tons on the coast (1707–08)

rows.name: Cowries
rows.route: India → Europe → West Africa

rows.name: Brass manillas
rows.route: Europe → West Africa. About 600 were found on the Whydah wreck

rows.name: Ivory ("Elephant's Teeth")
rows.route: West Africa → Europe (Lowther took it from the Greyhound, 1721)

rows.name: Trade cargo mix to Africa (cloth, iron, guns, spirits, beads)
rows.route: Proportions known only from a 1774–76 Bristol cargo (late); for 1650–1730: open

rows.name: Salt
rows.route: Turks Islands (Bermudians from the 1660s; Salt Cay 1673, Grand Turk 1678) → New England and Newfoundland fisheries. Salt Tortuga ("above 20 sail at a time", May–August; destination open). Bonaire → Curaçao. Cape Verde
rows.value: 20 bushels for "a few old clothes" at Sal

rows.name: Green turtle
rows.route: Cayman → Port Royal in sloops, kept in sea pens ("crawls"). The Port Royal market was "every day plentifully stored". Buccaneers lived on "tortoises"
rows.spoils: Kept alive so it stays fresh; salted turtle: open

rows.name: Boucan (smoked meat) and salted boar
rows.route: French Hispaniola hunters → Tortuga planters and ships
rows.value: Hunters were paid "two or three hundredweight of tobacco" for supplies

rows.name: Aromatic flowers and herbs; fragrant oils; perfume
rows.route: open
rows.sources: No period Caribbean trade found. A cultural or specialty good for one region: a flower-growing region and a perfume-making region give a reason to trade

rows.name: Seaweed
rows.route: open
rows.sources: No period trade found; use open

rows.name: Pewter plates and mugs
rows.route: open
rows.sources: Sourced (QAR, Part 2): 33 pieces on the Queen Anne's Revenge wreck, London touch-marks c. 1689–1712; pewterers at Port Royal. Added with the metal split

rows.name: Boats, sloops and ships; caulking and refit
rows.route: open
rows.sources: Sourced: the ship itself was the most valuable prize (Part 2); Bermuda cedar sloops from the mid-1600s; careening (DUTIES). Added with the wood split

rows.name: Pepper (black, white)
rows.route: Asia → Europe → the colonies. Lowther took "pepper" from a New England ship (1722)

rows.name: Cloves, nutmeg, mace, cinnamon
rows.route: Asia → Europe → the colonies; Ligon's cookery used cloves, mace and cinnamon; nutmeg grated on punch (Sloane)
rows.value: cloves 3.75, nutmeg 3.00, mace 8.40, cinnamon 3.00 guilders/lb, Amsterdam 1691

rows.name: Saffron
rows.route: Europe → the colonies

rows.name: Preserves, sugar candy, preserved ginger
rows.route: the islands and Europe; preserves need white sugar (L)
rows.value: white candy 0.50, preserved ginger 0.64 guilders/lb, Amsterdam 1691

rows.name: Aloes
rows.route: Barbados, Jamaica → London (35 lb in one month, 1681)

rows.name: Drug plants: sarsaparilla, china root, cassia fistula, tamarind, guaiacum
rows.route: Jamaica → London; Blome (1672) lists them among the island's commodities; guaiacum is lignum vitae (row 13)

rows.name: Peruvian bark (cinchona)
rows.route: Spanish Peru → Spain → London; sold by London chemists from 1658; Talbor's fever cure 1672–78

rows.name: Vanilla
rows.route: Spanish America (Campeche); "three pence a cod" (Dampier)

rows.name: Coffee
rows.route: Martinique (1723), Jamaica (1721/1728): planted at the very end of the period

rows.name: Tea
rows.route: Asia → England → the colonies; Roberts "drank his Tea constantly"

rows.name: Cassava, maize, yams, potatoes; cassava and potato bread
rows.route: the islands' own bread: "The third sort of bread we use, is only Potatoes" (L)

rows.name: Citrus (limes, oranges, lemons), pineapple, plantain
rows.route: the islands; limes "much fitter for sauce then the Limon"; "Pines worth all that went before" (L)

rows.name: Beer: small beer, ship's beer, strong beer and ale; cider
rows.route: England → ships and the islands: a gallon of beer a day by the Navy's 1678 contract; "Strong Beer 50 l." in Ligon's outlay; cider from New England and Virginia ("Apples and Sider" sold to Teach's sloop, J)
rows.package: hogshead (54 gal), tun ("seventy-five tuns of Beer and Ale", Barbados 1731, search only)
rows.spoils: beer spoils in the tropics; small beer "as bad as water bewitched" (Barlow 1667)

rows.name: Island drinks: mobbie, perino, grippo, beveridge, plantain drink, wine of pines
rows.route: made on Barbados by planters, housewives and Indian women; drunk there

rows.name: Punch, flip
rows.route: ships and punch-houses; punch is rum (or brandy, arrack), water, lime, sugar and nutmeg; flip is beer, spirit and sugar heated with a loggerhead

rows.name: Arrack
rows.route: East Indies → ships; "rum or arrack in lieu" of wine (Navy 1731); the pirates' liquor in the Indian Ocean
rows.value: small arrack "eleven perdos the keg" (16s 6d), Goa 1697

rows.name: Gum arabic
rows.route: West Africa: Senegal river escales → France, Holland (dyeing, calico printing)
rows.value: the French took 5,000 + 2,000 quintals a year; price open

rows.name: Beeswax
rows.route: West Africa: Senegal, Gambia, Sierra Leone, Gabon → Europe (candles); "there is always abundance of wax" (Barbot)
rows.value: bought with brandy, knives, iron bars; price open

rows.name: Malaguetta pepper (grains of paradise)
rows.route: West Africa: the Grain Coast, Rio Sestro → Bristol, London (a pepper substitute; ships' relish)
rows.value: "three hundred weight of it at Sestro for one bar of iron"

rows.name: Camwood
rows.route: West Africa: Sherbro, Cape Lopez → London dyers
rows.value: "about twenty five or thirty shillings per tun" at Cape Lopez

rows.name: Benin and Allada cloth
rows.route: West Africa: Benin → Dutch ships → the Gold Coast (for gold) and Angola

rows.name: Palm oil
rows.route: West Africa: Whydah, Calabar → ships (slave food, anointing); small export

rows.name: Kola nuts
rows.route: West Africa: Sierra Leone forest → Senegambia and the Sahel (chewed with salt and malaguetta; a gift)

rows.name: Loango copper; raffia cloth (libongo); redwood (takula); elephants' tails
rows.route: West-Central Africa: Loango, Mayumba, Kongo → Dutch, Luanda; libongo and macute were money at Luanda
rows.package: weight; cloth of 4 pieces; log; 100 hairs
rows.value: "an hundred hairs ... a thousand Reis, or six shillings"; ivory 5 libongos a lb; others open

rows.name: Cape Verde panos (strip cloth)
rows.route: Atlantic islands: Santiago, Fogo → the Rivers of Guinea, Senegal, Gambia as currency for slaves

rows.name: Orchil (urzela)
rows.route: Atlantic islands: Cape Verde, Canaries → Lisbon (a crown monopoly)

rows.name: Coast provisions: Indian corn and millet, yams, palm wine, dried fish, goats, fowls
rows.route: West Africa: Fante, Saboe, Whydah, Calabar → slave ships (Phillips loaded 700 chests of corn)
rows.value: palm wine 2s 3d per 5-gallon anchor; yams 14s a hundred; a goat 12–13s (Bosman)

rows.name: Trade beads: bugles, rangoes (carnelian), coral, amber
rows.route: Europe: Venice, Amsterdam, Genoa, Danzig, Cambay → the whole coast

rows.name: Brass basins, kettles and pans (battery ware); copper bars
rows.route: Europe: Bristol, Birmingham, Aachen → Whydah (cut into bracelets), Calabar, Senegal
rows.package: by weight; bar about 3 ft, 1¼ lb
rows.value: copper bars "from eighteen-pence to two shillings a-piece" (Barbot); 1 iron bar = 4 copper bars at Calabar

rows.name: Ready-made clothing and hats
rows.route: Europe: London → Barbados (a regiment's supply, 1668), Virginia (1693)
rows.value: hat 3s; shoes 2s 4d a pair; shirt 2s 6d; cravat 6d (1668)

rows.name: Earthenware, Delftware, glass bottles, window glass
rows.route: Europe: England, Delft (about 30 factories c. 1640–1740) → the colonies

rows.name: Paper, books
rows.route: Europe: England, the Zaan, Angoumois → the colonies

rows.name: Soap (Castile), wax candles
rows.route: Europe: Castile, England → the colonies

rows.name: Gunflints
rows.route: Europe: England → the colonies and Africa

rows.name: Coal (Newcastle sea-coal)
rows.route: Europe: the Tyne → London, Rotterdam, Flanders; the colonies

rows.name: Tradesmen's tool sets
rows.route: Europe: England → Virginia
rows.value: a carpenter's set about £1 10s; carpenter, cooper and joiner together £4 (17th c.)

rows.name: Gin (genever)
rows.route: Europe: Schiedam, Holland → England and abroad

rows.name: Herring
rows.route: Europe: the Dutch and Scots fisheries → Iberia, the Baltic, the Atlantic

rows.name: Whale oil (train oil) and whalebone
rows.route: Greenland (Dutch, 246 ships and 1,185 whales in 1684); North America: Long Island shore whaling (2,148 barrels in 1686–87, £4,300), Nantucket (1730: 25 vessels, 3,700 barrels); Newfoundland cod-liver train oil; Bahia (a crown monopoly) → Boston, London
rows.package: barrel, hogshead; sold by the ton
rows.value: oil about £2 a barrel, bone 6–8d a lb (Long Island); Newfoundland train oil £12 a ton, one hogshead per 40–64 quintals of fish

rows.name: Baltic stores: hemp, flax, masts, pitch, tar, Swedish iron and steel, Russian leather, Polish grain
rows.route: Europe: Riga, Stockholm, Petersburg, Danzig → Amsterdam → the west (Posthumus has the series: Riga hemp, Stockholm pitch, Muscovite tar, Swedish iron and steel, Polish wheat)
rows.value: open in the period (rye 88.90 guilders a last in 1572, early)

rows.name: Masts (white pine)
rows.route: North America: Piscataqua, from 1727 Casco Bay → the Royal Navy's yards; the Broad Arrow reserved trees of 24 inches
rows.package: mast ships of about 400 tons carrying 40–50 masts
rows.value: bounty £1 a mast (1705 Act); price open

rows.name: Olive oil
rows.route: Europe: Andalusia → the Indies by flota (11,077 arrobas in the 1706 flota), and to English and Dutch ports

rows.name: Mercury (quicksilver)
rows.route: Europe: Almadén → by barge to Cadiz → the flota → Mexico's silver mines (no local supply)

rows.name: Spanish merino wool
rows.route: Europe: Spain → Holland, England (Posthumus "Molina wool")

rows.name: Irish provisions: salt beef and pork, butter, tallow, hides
rows.route: Europe: Cork → the English and French islands, the navy; allowed direct by the 1663 Act; the Cattle Act 1667 pushed Ireland from live cattle to barrelled beef

rows.name: Bahia tobacco in rolls
rows.route: Brazil: the Recôncavo → Salvador → the Mina coast (lower grades, 15–20,000 three-arroba rolls) and Lisbon (the best); about 25,000 rolls a year 1700–10

rows.name: Brazilwood
rows.route: Brazil: the coast → Lisbon; a crown monopoly

rows.name: Brazilian gold and the moidore
rows.route: Brazil: Minas Gerais (found 1693/95) → Rio, Bahia → Lisbon → England; fintas 25–37 arrobas a year 1714–24; "800 metric tons" officially in the 18th century
rows.value: moidore about 27s in England (30s in Ireland); Roberts took 40,000 (J)

rows.name: Diamonds (Brazil, from 1729)
rows.route: Brazil: Serro do Frio → Lisbon → Amsterdam, London; a crown monopoly

rows.name: Cachaça (aguardente)
rows.route: Brazil: Bahia, Rio → Angola and Mina as trade liquor; coastwise

rows.name: Manioc flour (farinha)
rows.route: Brazil: coastwise and to Angola

rows.name: Mexican silver pesos
rows.route: Spanish America: the Mexico mint, 4,160,000 pesos a year 1665–1700 → Veracruz → Havana → Cadiz; Peru's silver by mule to Portobelo ("about 24,000,000 of pieces-of-eight", Dampier)
rows.value: the piece of eight 4s 6d intrinsic, 4s 3d at the exchangers (Newton 1711)

rows.name: Gold of New Granada and Darien
rows.route: Spanish America: the Chocó, Darien's rivers → Cartagena, Panama → Spain; output "at a very low level around 1675"

rows.name: Emeralds (Muzo)
rows.route: Spanish America: Muzo → Cartagena → Seville, and on to Mughal India

rows.name: Caracas cacao in detail
rows.route: Spanish America: La Guaira, Tucacas → Veracruz (New Spain ate most of it), Cadiz; by contraband → Curaçao → Amsterdam
rows.value: 6–8 pesos a fanega at source, about 100 in Europe

rows.name: Verina and Cuban tobacco; Seville snuff
rows.route: Spanish America: Verina "reputed the best in the world" (Dampier); Havana → the Seville snuff factory (1687); contraband to English and Dutch ships

rows.name: Spanish American drugs: jalap, balsam of Peru, balsam of Tolu, copal, liquidambar, sarsaparilla
rows.route: Spanish America: Honduras, Veracruz, Campeche, Cartagena → Cadiz; Spain imported 83,387 arrobas of drugs 1717–38 (5.6 t sarsaparilla, 1.6 t copal, 1 t balsams a year)

rows.name: Campeche wax, Yucatán cotton cloth, tasajo (jerked beef)
rows.route: Spanish America: Campeche, Sisal → Havana

rows.name: Mules and horses (Venezuela)
rows.route: Spanish America: Maracaibo, Tierra Firme → Curaçao, Saint-Domingue (for the sugar mills), Jamaica

rows.name: Beaver and the furs: marten, otter, fox, bear, raccoon

rows.name: Beaver hats
rows.route: North America: colonial hatters → other colonies, the islands, Iberia, until the Hat Act of 1732

rows.name: Deerskins in numbers (row 32)

rows.name: Newfoundland cod by grade (row 24)

rows.value: 7–8s a quintal (c. 1644); a boat took 200–300 quintals; servants £18–20 a season

rows.name: Ginseng
rows.route: North America: Mohawk country, Canada → Quebec → La Rochelle → Canton, exported from 1721

rows.name: Pig iron (colonial)

rows.name: Wampum

rows.name: Bermuda and Bahamas: cedar, onions, ambergris, braziletto, wrecked goods
rows.route: Atlantic islands: Bermuda → the islands and the mainland ports; New Providence, Eleuthera → Carolina, Jamaica; Spanish wrecks salvaged
rows.package: log; onions by the bunch; ambergris by the ounce

rows.name: Indentured servants
rows.route: Europe: England (Bristol, London), Ireland, Scotland → the Chesapeake (about 50,000 in 1630–80, three-quarters of arrivals) and the islands
rows.value: a carpenter's indenture valued £18 (1673); Newfoundland men £18–20 a season
